title: Tech leaders say AI means less work - their staff say they work up to 90 hours a week
description: For years now, executives at companies that are pouring hundreds of billions of dollars a year into developing various artificial intelligence tools h
body: For years now, executives at companies that are pouring hundreds of billions of dollars a year into developing various artificial intelligence tools have insisted that the technology will ultimately mean people will spend less of their time working.An engineering director at Google said four years ago that AI would deliver a four-day work week by 2025, external.Earlier this year, and just one year after that engineering director's prediction, OpenAI took up the challenge, in a manner of speaking. It formally urged companies to start testing out a four-day work week (with no change in pay), claiming that AI will soon be able to speed up so much human labour that the corporate world should prepare itself.However, a former OpenAI technical employee who left the company last year told the BBC the firm never actually trialled the four-day work week it suggested others should try while they were there.Instead, the person described what was often a gruelling work culture marked by frequent "crisis meetings", working on weekends, and "super cut-throat" performance reviews that would see colleagues suddenly let go."You go in on Saturday or Sunday just to catch up or make sure things aren't broken," the person said.Other companies have also pushed the idea that AI will effectively reduce the number of hours people need to work, for better or worse.Anthropic has boasted that its popular coding tool and chatbot Claude is capable of working on its own for seven hours without a break, external, essentially a full corporate workday. Meta's Mark Zuckerberg has said his company is in the middle of the year when "AI starts to dramatically change the way that we work" and that such tools let far fewer employees do more than they ever could have before.While Meta has since laid off 1 in 10 of its employees, Anthropic's chief executive Dario Amodei has warned that as AI tools inevitably become more productive, it could mean, external even broader job losses.Despite these claims, workers inside these same tech companies, who are not only developing but using the very AI tools that will purportedly perform at least some of people's work, say they are clocking in far more than the typical five-day, 40-hour work week.US tech workers are typically well-compensated, external, and while other industries such as investment banking, law and medicine also often see people work long hours, a 14-hour workday was not always the norm in tech. For years, it was a more typical 9-5 office job.But the former OpenAI employee said they would put in at least 70 hours a week, much more than they did in previous tech jobs. The person now works at a start-up also focused on AI, and said their work-life balance has improved, working closer to 50-60 hours a week, "outside of sprints".A "sprint" is term for a common period in technology companies in which people work long hours in the weeks leading up to a release of a new feature or product.Inside AI companies and larger tech companies working furiously on AI projects, however, such sprints can be extreme. At OpenAI and Anthropic, for instance, sprints can stretch on for many weeks and top 90 hours of work in a seven-day period, tech workers that the BBC spoke to for this story said.Neither company responded to BBC requests for comment. At Meta, workers said they have been abruptly pushed onto teams this year doing AI work being treated as urgent. They called it being "drafted", according to one current and one former employee, because people were not given a choice."They just move you over," the former employee said. "You can't say no – or if you do, you have to quit."They said although Meta recently began to walk back, external that strict take it or leave us approach, by then many workers had already been forced onto such work.The hours on such teams at Meta are often long, with staff working into the night, on weekends, and feeling they are "on call" during the hours they are not working, according to descriptions of the work from the current and former employees.There are no limits, external in the US on how many hours a person over the age of 16 can work. In the UK and Europe, for instance, laws limit a working week to 48 hours, including overtime.Meta's current AI projects include the creation of an AI tool that can be used for software engineering and other kinds of work, and building AI model infrastructure that can measure an AI model's success in replicating various tasks, the employees added."You're literally working in teams of people trying to replicate humans doing jobs," the former employee said.That work, the person added, seems "endless".A Meta spokesperson declined to comment.Even tech workers who are not directly involved in the development of AI tools are facing longer hours due to the technology.A former Google employee, Amin Shali, left the company in May due to the ways in which he claimed AI was negatively impacting his job, like having to often work all hours of the night because internal engineering functions had failed. This was happening more frequently as Google moved crucial resources like processing units and memory storage over to AI projects.A Google spokesperson declined to comment.Since leaving Google, Shali told the BBC that his sleep and overall health had improved. He said he's realised that heavy reliance on AI tools in large tech companies "creates a bad culture with excess pressure on engineers".Some new research suggests that AI tools are making people's workloads even more burdensome.A study, external out of UC Berkeley followed hundreds of workers at a US tech company for eight months as they used AI. It found the employees "worked at a faster pace, took on a broader scope of tasks, and extended work into more hours of the day".Neil Thompson, an innovation scholar at MIT, said that even at tech companies leading on AI development, it is unlikely that workers are being told to simply deploy the tools that are supposed to do some of their work and move on."It leads to a situation where even if there were real time savings, it would be sucked up by the changes, and implementing them, and making sure they worked," Thompson said.The UC Berkeley research found that the workload of tech employees was expanded in part because of the need to constantly check the output of AI tools.In a situation where an employee had smoothed out processes for AI tools, people also tend to fill any time saved with more work, Thompson added, either because they want to or they feel they should do in order to prove their value to an employer."People assume that 20% less work means four-day weeks," Thompson said. "But new work emerges."As Shali observed: "AI is supposed to be doing so much for us now, so many more people should at least have better health and better sleep."Instead, it seems to be the opposite.

schema.headline: Tech leaders say AI means less work - their staff say they work up to 90 hours a week

title: Ancient Roman shipwreck discovered off Sicily coast
description: Italian divers have discovered an ancient Roman shipwreck off the coast of Sicily, believed to be more than 2,000 years old.The vessel was found piled
body: Italian divers have discovered an ancient Roman shipwreck off the coast of Sicily, believed to be more than 2,000 years old.The vessel was found piled high with hundreds of well-preserved containers, which were used to transport goods such as wine and olive oil. Italy's Culture Minister Alessandro Giuli hailed the wreck as "one of the most important underwater archaeological discoveries of recent years".Specialist police divers found the ship around 46m (150ft) deep, after a tip-off from fishermen. The wreckage is 21m (69ft) long and 6m (20ft) wide, according to reports in local media.The culture ministry says it dates from the second or 1st Century BC. Fisherman and free-diver Giacomo De Mola described stumbling across the historic vessel while surveying the seabed near Mazara del Vallo.He wrote on social media that he had decided to dive and investigate after seeing something that appeared to be a large rock on his scanner. "I get closer. And my heart stops. It wasn't a rock," he said. Instead, he saw hundreds of amphorae - tall ceramic jars used to store goods in the ancient era, mostly wine, oil or grain."This is, without a doubt, the most incredible discovery of my life," he said. "It's hard to describe what it feels like to be among the first humans, in nearly 20 centuries, to see that place again."He posted a video of the wreck, showing eels, snappers and "countless marine life" living among the jars, noting: "The sea never ceases to amaze us. "This time we didn't just find a wreck, we found a piece of our history."

schema.headline: Ancient Roman shipwreck discovered off Sicily coast

title: Israel rejects Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, Netanyahu says
description: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected US President Donald Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, stating that no military pull-out will happ
body: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected US President Donald Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, stating that no military pull-out will happen until Hamas is "genuinely" disarmed.Trump's Board of Peace said last month it had reached an agreement for the "complete disarmament" of Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza.But Hamas said handing over its heavy weapons was contingent on Israel ending "all forms of aggression" and withdrawing its forces from Gaza.On Sunday, a senior Board of Peace official insisted the US-backed peace plan for the territory remained the only way forward.Israel has continued to carry out strikes on Gaza since agreeing to an initial ceasefire in the territory last October."Israel rejects the 15-point document," Netanyahu said at a cabinet meeting on Sunday.The Israeli military "will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens", he added. A Hamas official told the BBC on Sunday the group "reaffirms it commitment" to the agreement and it was ready "to engage seriously and responsibly in implementing" the 15-point plan.They called on mediators to ensure "that all parties comply with what has been agreed".Israel's rejection signals another blow for Trump's Gaza peace plan which was announced in September last year.The plan included the creation of the Board of Peace to oversee the agreement's implementation, as well as the disarmament of Hamas, withdrawal of Israeli troops and reconstruction of Gaza.Netanyahu's statement does not come as a surprise. But he has taken some time to make it, perhaps reflecting the difficult position the Israeli leader is in.He clearly is unhappy with Trump's plan but at the same time he will not want to upset his closest ally.It's just over a week since Trump announced what he called a "monumental step toward lasting peace and security" - that Hamas for the first time had agreed to disarm, on condition that Israel withdraws its forces from Gaza.On Sunday, Netanyahu was clear that was not going to happen under his watch. He said Hamas had to disarm first, adding that it couldn't be some "fictitious disarmament" - it had to be real.The reality is any disarmament and withdrawal of Israeli forces would likely need to be phased.Netanyahu said he was now in discussion with US officials about how to go forward. "They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand our ground on these matters," he said.But just months before Israeli elections and under pressure from members of his right-wing coalition to take a tough stance on Gaza, he is unlikely to want to make concessions.He has faced calls from far-right parts of the coalition to hold a new cabinet vote and end the Gaza plan, including National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir who dismissed the draft as "not acceptable".Nickolay Mladenov - a senior diplomat tasked with implementing Donald Trump's peace plan - defended the plan on Sunday and said discussions were ongoing in the hope of a "positive outcome".The board's high representative for Gaza told Israel's Channel 12 that Israel had been asked "to give the process a chance" and said the plan was "the only way forward" to ensure there was no repeat of the 7 October 2023 attack by Hamas.Mladenov said the plan was built on a process that was "verifiable, that is reversible, that at each stage can be stopped, and that we have built up with a very clear-eyed understanding of what are the challenges ahead".He also said that Israel would not be required to withdraw until it could be verified that Hamas was taking steps to disarm.According to the United Nations, about 1.9 million people - 90% of Gaza's population - have been displaced in the territory since the war in Gaza started. The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.Israel responded to the attack by launching a military campaign in Gaza, during which more than 73,000 people have been killed, according to the territory's health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.Additional reporting by Jack Burgess

schema.headline: Israel rejects Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, Netanyahu says

title: Jose Mourinho agreed to replace Sir Alex Ferguson at Man Utd in 2013
description: After years of speculation, Jose Mourinho has confirmed that he agreed to replace Sir Alex Ferguson at Manchester United in 2013, before changing his
body: After years of speculation, Jose Mourinho has confirmed that he agreed to replace Sir Alex Ferguson at Manchester United in 2013, before changing his mind and re-joining Chelsea instead."When I left Real Madrid, I signed to go to Manchester United after Sir Alex," the 63-year-old coach - now back at Real for a second spell - said in a new Netflix documentary series about his career."He was offered the job, yes," confirmed Ferguson, who won 13 Premier League titles over 26 years at Old Trafford before retiring in 2013."I sat him down and explained the situation," he added: "As far as I was concerned, he was accepting. And then, within hours, it changed."What changed was that Mourinho felt he could not turn down a return to Chelsea, where he had won consecutive Premier League titles in 2005 and 2006."One night, he phoned me and he was crying and he says, 'Alex, I can't take it. I've given my word to Chelsea and I'm not going to break my word'," said the former United boss."The reason he gave to me, I could understand, but I was disappointed."Mourinho said he was "very flattered" to be offered the job of replacing Ferguson "because Manchester United has an incredible appeal"."But one thing is love for football, another thing is love for a certain club," he explained."I think this is more powerful than love for football and fundamentally, after Real Madrid, I needed to feel that I'm loved."For me to lose the chance to be the coach to succeed Sir Alex Ferguson was dramatic, but I don't regret (it) because it was a decision that I made with my heart."After returning to Stamford Bridge in 2013, Mourinho went on to win his third Premier League title as well as the League Cup.In May 2016, he got a second chance to take over at United, succeeding Louis van Gaal. Over a two-and-a-half year spell at Old Trafford, Mourinho won League Cup and Europa League titles before being sacked in December 2018 following a slump in results.He returned to another of his old clubs, Real Madrid, in May this year. Mourinho's last spell there ended in acrimony as he fell out with club captain Iker Casillas and other players. On the eve of his Real reunion, the combative manager and former Spain goalkeeper Casillas spoke candidly about the reasons behind those differences.Mourinho also spoke about difficulties he has faced with former Chelsea owner Roman Abramovich, who hired him twice and sacked him both times.After taking over a struggling Real side, Mourinho helped them challenge the dominance of Pep Guardiola's Barcelona, winning La Liga, Copa del Rey and Spanish Super Cup trophies in his first two seasons at the Bernabeu. The 100 points they amassed in 2011-12 remains a La Liga record.However, the wheels came off in Mourinho's third season in the Spanish capital and he was dismissed at the end of 2012-13 with Real finishing 15 points behind rivals Barcelona.His treatment of Casillas divided the dressing room. The goalkeeper made 725 appearances across 25 years at Real, winning three Champions League titles and five La Liga crowns, but had spent much of the 2012-13 season on the bench."The relationship Jose and I had was very cold," he said."In those years, I really think it was taken to a limit where in the end, the rope broke."Former Real midfielder Sami Khedira said that Mourinho's rift with Casillas affected everyone."Iker is a Real Madrid legend, loved by every Real Madrid supporter. He benched him, doesn't speak to him, spoke bad about him in the media, so then this locker room was a nightmare, honestly," he said."After that, the relationship between Jose and many, many players was broken – like Cristiano [Ronaldo] and the Spanish guys, Casillas, Sergio Ramos. And those players were super, super important for the atmosphere in the locker room."Mourinho claimed that the keeper had a bad attitude."The first three times that I spoke to Casillas, the captain, the first thing he told me was, 'I want to ask for more holidays for the national team players'," he said."The second time he spoke to me was, 'I would like to ask you to put the training sessions one hour later because at the time you want the training sessions, there is a lot of traffic in Madrid'. The third time he comes to speak with me was, 'We don't want to go to [the] hotel. We prefer just to meet on matchday and go direct to the stadium to play'. And in a short period of time, I realised they're spoilt."Former Spain captain Casillas also revealed that he clashed with Mourinho over the manager's attitude towards his international team-mates who played for Barcelona.The 63-year-old's response was unapologetic."There are things that I don't accept and I will never accept and when somebody doesn't respect me, it's a problem. I say, this is Barcelona, Real Madrid. When you go to the national team, then you can kiss the guy, but not now. This is war."Mourinho was sacked by Abramovich at Chelsea in 2007 and 2015.The veteran manager said that his former boss became increasingly interfering during his first spell at the club, including pushing for the signing of Andriy Shevchenko. The Ukraine striker joined Chelsea in May 2006 for a then club record fee of approximately £30m, but scored only nine league goals in 48 games over a three-year spell in West London."Abramovich - incredible passion for football, but knowing nothing about the situation," Mourinho said."Shevchenko was on the table because of connections with the boss, connections with agents and I never wanted to sign him, but I never told no one, so it's also my responsibility. You want to know the player that I wanted? [Samuel] Eto'o."Following his dismissal by the Russian oligarch in September 2007, Mourinho had a chance for revenge when he returned to Stamford Bridge in February 2010 with Inter Milan in the last 16 of the Champions League. The Italian side beat Chelsea 2-1, before going on to win the title."Honestly, I was playing against Roman that game," Mourinho said."I was playing against a guy that sacked me. I go home happy and he goes home upset. Because I know how much he loved Chelsea, I know how much he loves to win."But I needed revenge, because football belongs to people like me. The other ones are the intruders that don't belong. Football belongs to the players, belongs to the coaches, belongs to the fans. Football will always belong to us."

schema.headline: Jose Mourinho agreed to replace Sir Alex Ferguson at Man Utd in 2013

title: Rangers: Derek McInnes left frustrated amid poor start to season
description: After their Europa League qualifying loss in Poland, McInnes called on his side to "be far more stingy with our work, defend the goal with our lives,
body: After their Europa League qualifying loss in Poland, McInnes called on his side to "be far more stingy with our work, defend the goal with our lives, don't give our opponent opportunities" and criticised the squad for showing the same worrying characteristics that were the club's ruin last season.His side showed little sign of turning this around in the short space of time since their European trip.Against Hibs on Sunday afternoon, his third different back four of the season struggled to hold their shape and summer signing Vanja Dragojevic soon grappled Josh Kerr to the ground for a penalty as the errors continued.These faults, coupled with a lack of consistency in playing partners, is compounding the misery.Their draw with Dundee United started with a back-line comprising of Ben Godfrey, Dujon Sterling, Emmanuel Fernandez and Tuur Rommens.Away in Poland, it was Ross McCrorie, Sterling, Emmanuel Fernandez and Rommens.When David Gray's team came to town it was Dragojevic, Olwethu Makhanya, Fernandez and Rommens.These issues need to be ironed out quickly by the coaching staff as their Europa League qualification hangs in the balance prior to Thursday's second leg against Jagiellonia Bialystok.McInnes thought the defeat by Hibs was "really harsh on us" as "we were the better team" and "deserved far better than we got" in a game in which Hibs took the lead through a penalty he disputed."It's damaging in the sense that we came here to win and we expect to win," he said."What we've got to do now is just dust ourselves down because that was a blow for us."The response of the team in the latter part of the game was terrific."Their selection inconsistency is mirrored in their form on the park too.Allan added: "Performing consistently is what [brings] results and winning silverware, and I know its very early on, but there is no consistency in how Rangers were playing today."A McInnes side throughout his spells in charge of St Johnstone, Aberdeen, Kilmarnock and Hearts could all be described as hard to beat.This early iteration of his Rangers squad are the opposite.The 55-year-old has now lost more home league games in charge of Rangers as he did in his whole time as Tynecastle boss.As former Ibrox midfielder Ryan Jack suggested: "For Rangers to be at home in their first league home game of the season, Derek McInnes' first home game in charge and to score thtough a Hibs own goal and not create too much with two strikers on the park will be frustrating."I touched on it before the game, if you go one without a win it's trouble, then two, now three, usually that's crisis time and people start asking serious questions."It's early on in Derek McInnes' reign and a lot of new players are in, so you need time for that to gel, but as you do that, you need to pick up results as this football club demands it."With nine signings already in the building, McInnes wants to further bolster his squad. With Youssef Chermiti being taken off on a stretcher on the day it was revealed Rangers had rejected a big-money offer for the striker, that may complicate matters further.Especially as it appeared that another winger and extra defenders were the manager's priorities.Speaking pre-match, the manager said: "We've got a few bids in for several players and a few things are ongoing at the minute."Ideally, a lot of these things would have came to fruition a wee bit quicker."But hopefully, if there is any news to tell, it'll be in the upcoming days on a few of our targets."

schema.headline: Rangers: Derek McInnes left frustrated amid poor start to season

title: Newspaper headlines: 'New prisons outrage' and 'Days of danger'
description: The government's chief post-Brexit negotiator tells the Guardian, external that the UK will "move faster" toward closer ties with Europe under Andy Bu
body: The government's chief post-Brexit negotiator tells the Guardian, external that the UK will "move faster" toward closer ties with Europe under Andy Burnham. Hamish Falconer says there's "room to be ambitious" within Labour's red lines on Europe, which exclude reopening discussions on the single market and customs union.Chinese spy cameras have been found on Royal Navy drones used by elite special forces, according to a report in the Daily Telegraph, external. It says components made in China were able to transmit data back to Beijing. The Ministry of Defence tells the paper there's no evidence any sensitive data or systems had been sent abroad.A report in the Times, external claims Prime Minister Andy Burnham is struggling to convince one of his closest allies to join his government because of differing opinions on wealth taxes. According to the paper, Lord O'Neill, a former Goldman Sachs economist and Treasury minister, has been offered significant roles but has previously said he is "very opposed" to wealth taxes because they could be "easily gamed".The Financial Times, external leads on claims from some former CIA officials, who've accused President Trump of following an "autocrat's playbook" and leaving the US "less safe". One tells the paper US democratic "guardrails" have been taken down and adds: "I don't think we're close to the worst of where we're going to". A White House official is quoted as saying Donald Trump puts "American citizens first".The Daily Mail, external, citing figures compiled by the Conservative Party, says 89,000 more crimes will be committed across Britain as a result of the government's prisoner early release scheme. "Sex offenders, robbers and arsonists will cause mayhem" reads its front page. A Ministry of Justice spokesperson dismisses the data as highly speculative and inaccurate.Car washes and private membership swimming pools could face water bans in the next heatwave according to the i Paper, external. It says some water firms are preparing "non-essential" restrictions for the first time in twenty years. The Daily Mirror, external focuses on warnings from bereaved families of the dangers of open water swimming during the hot weather.And the Metro, external leads on the prime minister bringing forward new rules to make it easier to cancel subscriptions. "Andy wants a cancel culture", reads its headline.

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: 'New prisons outrage' and 'Days of danger'

title: Travelodge staff gave domestic abuser key to his victim's room
description: A domestic violence victim has told BBC Breakfast how she was attacked in her hotel room after Travelodge reception staff gave a key to her abuser.The
body: A domestic violence victim has told BBC Breakfast how she was attacked in her hotel room after Travelodge reception staff gave a key to her abuser.The woman, whom the BBC is calling Lucy, said she was "failed" by the chain and described it as one of the "most traumatic nights of my life" after the man kicked the door off its hinges.She contacted the BBC after hearing about the sentencing of Kyran Smith, who sexually assaulted a woman in her bed at a Travelodge in Maidenhead in 2022.Speaking about Lucy's case, Travelodge said that while incidents like this were "very rare", customer safety and security was, and remained, a priority with staff undergoing recent training.Lucy said she was staying at the hotel in October 2025 for "a night away from the fear" following a period of abuse that left her "frightened and exhausted"."He walked into the hotel and told the receptionist that his girlfriend was upstairs having a seizure. He asked what room I was in and what floor I was staying on," she said.The receptionist handed him a key before directing him upstairs to Lucy's room, she said."I couldn't believe it. The one place I thought he could never get to, he had somehow reached. I felt sick with panic. My safe place disappeared in an instant," she added.She said he physically attacked her and tried to grab her phone.After Lucy convinced her attacker to leave, he returned, "banging, shouting and becoming more aggressive"."I was absolutely terrified. I froze, hoping he would stop. Instead, he kicked the hotel room door off its hinges and forced his way back inside."She said she ran downstairs "shaking, crying and begging for help", adding: "I thought someone would protect me."Instead, Lucy was offered another room in the hotel.Another woman, Jo from Leeds, contacted BBC News following coverage of the Maidenhead attack.In July, she woke in her room to an unknown man standing at the end of her bed, and screamed for help."It was just horrible, it was horrendous. Terrifying. I was shaking so badly," she said.Her friend who was staying in the room heard him say, "I'm sorry, they gave me this key," she said.Jo considered staying elsewhere following the reports of the attack in 2022, but was reassured by Travelodge's chief executive Jo Boydell, who previously said: "The safety and security of customers in our hotels is extremely important and we want everyone to be safe, and feel safe, in our hotels."Jo said: "What happened to us shouldn't have happened. And the assurances [Travelodge] gave are not accurate. The systems are failing."In response, Travelodge said an investigation found "our updated room access security policies, which were in place at the time, were not correctly followed, which is not acceptable."We have retrained the hotel team on our current room security and check-in procedures."Andy Smith, who has travelled the country with his band and stays in dozens of Travelodge hotels a year, said he had been given keys to other people's rooms recently."On Friday, we went up to the room and there was a guy already asleep in there in a state of undress," he said.It followed another incident about 18 months ago where another man had gained access to his room by telling reception staff he was checking in under a common name such as "Mr Smith", Smith said."I think he just chanced it. Because my name's Smith, I think it's just the pure luck of it. I mean, why wouldn't anyone be asking for ID or anything, like a booking reference or an email address. It's beggar's belief."Travelodge responded by saying "any case of an unauthorised person entering a guest's room is a significant cause for concern and we want to be clear that these incidents should not have happened".A spokesperson for industry group UKHospitality said recent incidents were "extremely serious" and it understood the concerns from guests.It was working with its members to create guidance on customer security which would be published shortly, the spokesperson said."Developed with sector experts, we have continued to engage with ministers on this important work and received positive feedback from government on the work taking place to further bolster guest security," they said.Travelodge said it had commissioned an independent review led by a barrister "to examine our room access security policies and escalation procedures"."While the independent review is progressing, we have also conducted an internal review and have since made changes to our room access security policy and incident escalation procedures supported by training for all of our customer-facing colleagues."Lucy said the night of her attack had "changed me forever", and she was now unable to stay in hotels because of the fear and anxiety she feels."Hotels need safeguarding procedures... because one mistake can have devastating consequences," she said.If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.

schema.headline: Travelodge staff gave domestic abuser key to his victim's room

title: The Hundred 2026 results: Sunrisers Leeds close to qualification after Welsh Fire win
description: The Hundred men's competition, HeadingleySunrisers Leeds 201-4 (100 balls): Marsh 50 (34); Woakes 2-41Welsh Fire 130-6 (100 balls): Short 43 (29); Car
body: The Hundred men's competition, HeadingleySunrisers Leeds 201-4 (100 balls): Marsh 50 (34); Woakes 2-41Welsh Fire 130-6 (100 balls): Short 43 (29); Carse 3-24Sunrisers Leeds won by 71 runsScorecard. TableSunrisers Leeds moved closer to securing qualification for The Hundred's knockout stages with a comprehensive 71-run win over Welsh Fire.Mitch Marsh, the tournament's leading run-scorer, struck his fourth half-century of the season for second-placed Sunrisers as they made 201-4 at Headingley.The Australian opener hit a 34-ball 50 and added 89 for the first wicket with Ryan Rickelton.Chris Woakes, who took 2-41, claimed the breakthrough when he had Rickelton caught for 40, while Harry Brook (23 from 11 balls) and Marsh fell within the space of five deliveries, caught off Jordan Clark and Lockie Ferguson respectively.Captain Zak Crawley struck four sixes in a 12-ball 34 as Sunrisers pressed on, while Dan Lawrence (29) and Matthew Revis (15) ended the innings with an unbroken partnership of 27.Fifth-placed Fire were unable to keep up with the required run-rate in their reply as only Matt Short (43) and Joe Root (31), who put on 49 for the second wicket, made more than 13.Short was one of three victims for Brydon Carse, who also removed opener Phil Salt (13) and Marco Jansen (1).Root was caught behind off Nathan Ellis, who also bowled Rachin Ravindra for two, while Jordan Cox also fell cheaply, caught for 12 off Matthew Potts.Tom Kohler-Cadmore and Woakes both finished unbeaten on 13 as Fire closed on 130-6, well short of their target having chosen to chase at the toss.Sunrisers now only need to avoid defeat against Manchester Super Giants on Tuesday to progress, while victory would put them in contention for top spot should leaders Trent Rockets lose against Southern Brave on Monday.Fire, who would have moved second with a win on Sunday, are the lowest placed of three teams on 16 points and will likely need success against London Spirit on Wednesday and then rely on net run-rate to secure the final knockout spot.The Hundred men's competition, HeadingleyBirmingham Phoenix 162-4 (100 balls): Clarke 73 (42), Dickson 51 (28); Crocombe 1-8London Spirit 166-3 (82 balls): Livingstone 66 (30), Brevis 55 (31); Thompson 1-24London Spirit won by seven wicketsScorecard. TableDewald Brevis and Liam Livingstone shared a 103-run partnership as London Spirit beat Birmingham Phoenix by seven wickets at Lord's.In a match between two eliminated sides, Livingstone hit 66 from 30 balls, while Brevis struck an unbeaten 55 from 31 as Spirit passed their target of 163 with 18 balls to spare.Coming together at 43-2 after the hosts had lost Jonny Bairstow and Lhuan-dre Pretorius for 10 and 16 respectively, the pair struck a collective total of 12 fours and seven sixes, hitting the ball deep into the stands on multiple occasions.Home captain Livingstone skied a catch to Sean Dickson off Tom Helm, but Brevis saw Spirit home alongside James Coles (9), striking back-to-back fours to first reach his half-century and then end the match.Phoenix reached what appeared to be a competitive score after being put into bat, with opener Joe Clarke scoring 73 from 42 deliveries and Dickson hitting an unbeaten 51 from 28.The pair put on a third-wicket stand of 92 after Mitch Owen, Joe Weatherley and Laurie Evans had all fallen for single figures, while Clarke ultimately departed from the 91st ball of the innings, caught by Livingstone off Henry Crocombe.Phoenix's sixth defeat in seven matches mean they stay bottom of The Hundred standings, while Spirit moved level with sixth-placed Southern Brave on eight points, but remain beneath them by virtue of an inferior net run-rate.Nottingham is the venue for Monday's action in The Hundred with Trent Rockets hosting Southern Brave.The match for the women's side at 15:00 BST is a top-of-the-table clash, with leaders Rockets aiming to clinch their place in the Lord's final.Victory over Brave in their final match would secure their spot, although given they have a superior net run-rate they could go directly to Lord's even if they lose.Second-placed Brave are in a strong position to secure a place in the Eliminator - and would be certain if they win.The Rockets' men's side will also secure their spot in the final on 16 August with victory over Brave in their match which gets under way at 18:00.Brave are playing for pride, having already been eliminated and victory would guarantee they avoid the wooden spoon.You can follow ball-by-ball commentary on both matches on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra, BBC Sounds and the BBC Sport website and app.

schema.headline: The Hundred 2026 results: Sunrisers Leeds close to qualification after Welsh Fire win

title: Hot weather reveals hidden history across the South
description: Image source, Pete SeawardImage caption, The outline of an 18th Century garden is visible on a lawn at Blenheim PalaceByEthan GudgeSouth of EnglandAs
body: Image source, Pete SeawardImage caption, The outline of an 18th Century garden is visible on a lawn at Blenheim PalaceByEthan GudgeSouth of EnglandAs the south of England continues to enjoy an unusually warm and dry summer, parch marks on lawns across the region have revealed the hidden histories of their location.Among the sites which have seen the outlines of historic installations exposed by the hot weather are Portchester Castle and Blenheim Palace.At Blenheim, the footprint of an 18th Century garden - which had once stretched across the width of the entire palace - has revealed itself on a lawn.Andy Mills, the Unesco World Heritage Site's head gardener, told the BBC it was "absolutely magical" to see the outlines of the historic parterre - 260 years after it was demolished.Mills explained that the original parterre - which is a French word meaning "on the ground" - had been constructed in 1705, and would have "cost an absolute fortune to install"."It was a very large extravagant thing to do, but it was a way of showing your wealth and importance and that sort of thing," he said.Image source, Blenheim PalaceImage caption, The original plans for the parterre at Blenheim show its scaleBut the garden was dismantled in 1760, only leaving its outline to be revealed in spells of particularly hot weather."The footprint of it has appeared out on the lawn, and it is absolutely fantastic - it's a huge structure, it's just massive," Mills said."We know it's there, we know it's under the ground, we know the archaeology is there and it's just one of those happy coincidences of this very, very hot weather that these things appear.""It's just superb to see - it's amazing."Image source, National TrustImage caption, The outlines of some lost buildings at Greys Court - near Henley-on-Thames - have also been uncoveredElsewhere in Oxfordshire, the weather has also revealed the outline of some lost buildings at Greys Court - near Henley-on-Thames.The parch marks show a range of 16th Century buildings which had once stood on the National Trust property's Oval Lawn.Archeological enquiries at the site in recent years have discovered that the outlines belonged to a long, narrow building which once stood on the lawn and linked two sides of a medieval courtyard.Image source, English HeritageImage caption, The footprint of a Tudor storehouse at Portchester Castle has been revealed by the warm weatherMeanwhile, at Portchester Castle in Hampshire, the warm conditions have led to parch marks revealing the outline of a Tudor storehouse.English Heritage, which runs the castle, said the storehouse was believed to date from between 1489 and 1540.Image source, National TrustImage caption, Parch marks at Mottisfont show the remains of 13th and 16th Century wall foundationsMottisfont, near Romsey, has also experienced similar marks this summer - uncovering the remains of 13th and 16th Century wall foundations.The National Trust said the walls were the "buried remains of monastery buildings including a cloister and various other buildings, as well as later Tudor alterations".Archaeologist James Brown said the outlines were "intriguing glimpses into the oldest history of buildings known" at Mottisfont."We have carried out some geophysical surveys but the buildings have never been dug so their secrets remain hidden except for these rare moments when their outlines appear in the lawns," he added.Get in touchYour Voice

schema.headline: Hot weather reveals hidden history across the South

title: Risk of patient safety 'bonfire' with Health Bill changes, Lib Dems say
description: The Liberal Democrats have urged Andy Burnham to stop the "bonfire of patient safety" as part of the government's plans to modernise the NHS. Healthwa
body: The Liberal Democrats have urged Andy Burnham to stop the "bonfire of patient safety" as part of the government's plans to modernise the NHS. Healthwatch England (HWE), an independent body which represents the views of patients at their local health and social care providers, is set to be scrapped under the NHS Modernisation Bill. The Health Service Safety Investigation Bureau (HSSIB), which carries out patient safety investigations, is also being abolished. The government says its changes will strip back bureaucracy and improve patient safety. The Lib Dems warned it risks another Stafford Hospital scandal – where years of abuse and neglect led to hundreds of unnecessary patient deaths. A Healthcare Commission report found the scandal – one of the biggest in NHS history – involved at least 400 more deaths than expected between 2005 and 2008. Under the government proposals, Healthwatch's responsibilities will be transferred to integrated care boards (ICBs) and local authorities, meaning they would have to respond to feedback about their own services, rather than being challenged by an independent body.Separately, HSSIB's functions will be transferred to the government-run Care Quality Commission (CQC), which the Lib Dems argue raises concerns there is no guarantee that staff who raise safety concerns are given anonymity.Other measures include the abolition of NHS England in a bid to centralise the running of health and social care services under the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC).The government says this will reduce bureaucracy and allow more resources to be delivered to frontline healthcare services.The NHS Modernisation Bill is currently at the report stage and due for a third reading on 7 September. Liberal Democrat health spokesperson Helen Morgan said this was "a catastrophic step backwards" and described it as the "greatest backward step in patient safety in a generation". "Andy Burnham must urgently put an end to this, and fix the Health Bill so that modernising the NHS doesn't come at the expense of accountability, transparency or patient safety," Morgan added.In a speech on NHS reform in January, then-Health Secretary Wes Streeting said "there are many decent people working at Healthwatch who care, but the job of listening to patients can't be farmed out to an arm's length body". "It must be core business for the NHS. That is why we're taking it back in-house and I won't back down on that either." The Lib Dems also said the current bill removes the duty for the NHS to cooperate with the Care Quality Commission in providing key safety data and removes automatic "safe space" protections for whistleblowers. Amendments tabled by the Liberal Democrats would cancel the changes and the party is "urging the new Burnham administration to adopt them".The party vowed to robustly fight the government in the House of Lords, where Labour doesn't have a majority.A DHSC spokesperson said NHS Modernisation Bill "explicitly preserves safe space provisions and staff will continue to be protected"."The reforms we are introducing will give patients a stronger, clearer voice at the heart of health and social care." Burnham was health secretary in 2009, when the Healthcare Commission's report was released on the Stafford Hospital scandal. Burnham then launched an independent inquiry in 2010.In May, the Local Government Association (LGA) told the BBC disbanding Healthwatch would be a "significant step back" in accountability."Without an independent, locally rooted voice to challenge and represent communities, there is a risk of duplication and gaps in accountability," the LGA said. There are currently more than 150 local Healthwatch organisations in England.

schema.headline: Risk of patient safety 'bonfire' with Health Bill changes, Lib Dems say

title: Harry Potter fans force power link diversion to avoid Dobby's grave
description: He said a colleague told him the nature of the calls, and that "apparently we're going to go straight through Dobby's grave"."I said 'Dobby, who's Dob
body: He said a colleague told him the nature of the calls, and that "apparently we're going to go straight through Dobby's grave"."I said 'Dobby, who's Dobby? I don't know Dobby?'"I said 'he's a fictitious character in a fictitious book, the whole thing is fictitious what are you talking about?'"[The colleague] said 'no it's very, very serious'."Ludlam said he then discussed with planners "exactly how to reroute the cable so we wouldn't go anywhere close to Dobby's grave".He added: "A lot of people were very happy about that, and the project is now going [ahead] and Dobby's happy."The Bronze Age remains the cable went close to were mentioned in Pembrokeshire council planning documents, external about the power link.It said archaeological trenches dug near the route of the underground cable "contained the rim of an inverted pottery vessel whose fabric suggests a Bronze Age collared urn circa 1700-1500BC, typically associated with human burial".The cable diversion is not the first time Dobby's grave has been saved.In 2022 the National Trust agreed it could remain in place following a consultation,  but urged visitors not to leave souvenirs.Fans were asked not to leave socks on the mock grave, made of pebbles with messages written on them, because the beach was environmentally sensitive.

title: Typhoon Dolphin: China evacuates more than 1 million people as massive storm arrives
description: Chinese authorities have evacuated more than a million people from their homes in eastern China including Shanghai, as Typhoon Dolphin made landfall.I
body: Chinese authorities have evacuated more than a million people from their homes in eastern China including Shanghai, as Typhoon Dolphin made landfall.It packed maximum wind speeds of 150km/h (94mph) when it first slammed into Yuhuan in the Zhejiang province at 17:30 (09:30 GMT) before making a second landfall in the city of Wenzhou about an hour later, meteorological authorities said.The typhoon halted transportation across the region – 1,400 flights were cancelled in Shanghai alone.Chinese authorities had earlier issued their highest-level red alert for Dolphin, but by Monday morning they downgraded it to a tropical storm.The storm is moving inland within China, and authorities are still warning of torrential rains, severe flooding and the risk of landslides through to Wednesday.Heavy rain was forecast on Monday for the provinces of Shandong, Henan, Hubei, Anhui, Jiangsu, Zhejiang and the city of Shanghai.Local governments have urged people to avoid outdoor activities, while several top tourist attractions remain closed, including parts of Disneyland and Legoland, and several viewing platforms along the Bund in Shanghai.Footage on state media show ground-floor businesses flooded in the former French Concession in Shanghai - an area popular with tourists - and people walking through ankle-deep waters.Several state media outlets have reported that a nine-year-old boy from Wenling, Zhejiang is missing after being swept into the sea. Chinese officials have not reported any casualties.Parts of Zhejiang could receive 250mm to 500mm of rain over the next few days, forecasters say.Authorities in Hangzhou, Zhejiang's capital city, have waived parking fees in all public spaces for drivers seeking shelter amid the strong winds and floodwaters.Elsewhere in the province, Wenzhou authorities have relocated some 900,000 residents and opened more than 1,000 emergency shelters, while about 390,000 people have been evacuated from their homes in the city of Taizhou.In the coastal province of Fujian, maritime authorities have suspended dozens of passenger ferry routes and halted more than 100 offshore construction projects.The storm moved over a long distance of 6,000km before making landfall, suggesting a lifespan of more than three times that of an average typhoon, according to China's state broadcaster CCTV. It also has a massive cirulation size and intense rainfall capacity, CCTV reported.

schema.headline: Typhoon Dolphin: China evacuates more than 1 million people as massive storm arrives

title: Daniel Kinahan: Suspected crime boss appears before Special Criminal Court
description: Suspected crime boss Daniel Kinahan appears in court after extraditionImage source, SolarpixImage caption, Kinahan, pictured here in 2010, was extradi
body: Suspected crime boss Daniel Kinahan appears in court after extraditionImage source, SolarpixImage caption, Kinahan, pictured here in 2010, was extradited to the Republic of Ireland on SundayByGabija GataveckaiteDublin correspondentEimear Flanagan and Barry O'ConnorBBC News NISuspected crime boss Daniel Kinahan, one of the world's most wanted men, has appeared before a Dublin court after being extradited from Dubai.He has been charged with directing the activities of a criminal organisation between 18 October 2015 and 6 April 2017.An Irish government jet carrying the 49-year-old landed in Dublin after 18:00 local time. He was arrested and charged upon his arrival.Following a 13-minute non-jury hearing at the Special Criminal Court, he was remanded in custody until 5 October.Kinahan was arrested in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in April. He appealed the extradition order over the past few months but his attempts were unsuccessful.The National Crime Agency (NCA) has previously said that the Kinahan cartel has been responsible for importing tonnes of drugs and firearms around the world and has also been linked to more than a dozen gangland murders.Kinahan was not only wanted by the authorities in Ireland - the US Treasury Department once described the Kinahan cartel as one of the most dangerous in the world.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Daniel Kinahan arrived into Casement Aerodrome in Baldonnel, Dublin on the government jet on Sunday eveningThe US government imposed sanctions on Kinahan in April 2022 after identifying him and other members of his family as leaders of the Kinahan organised crime cartel.He fought attempts to extradite him back to his native country, where the Kinahan cartel was involved in a long-running gangland feud that claimed 18 lives.A large-scale security operation was in place ahead of Sunday's hearing.Ahead of the extradition, the Irish Prison Service bought a bulletproof and bombproof van which can be used to escort prisoners who are considered high-risk.Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly said the arrest shows the force's determination to "target transnational organised crime groups" alongside international policing partners such as Dubai police.He added it shows the value of the force's relationship with the authorities in the UAE, the Irish ministry of justice at judicial level, and "on a police-to-police basis".'I won't be getting bail'Image source, PA MediaImage caption, A police convoy escorted Kinahan at speed to the courtKinahan arrived at Baldonnell Casement Aerodrome on Sunday evening, where gardaí arrested and charged him.He was directly transported under heavy police guard to the Criminal Courts of Justice in Dublin.All the benches were full in a packed courtroom of journalists, a number of solicitors from the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP), some members of the public and court clerks.In court, Kinahan was sitting on a wooden bench and wearing a black hooded top.He appeared before judges Patrick McGrath, Sarah Berkeley and Fiona Lydon, and rose to his feet when the three judges took their places.Image source, Mike O'DonnellImage caption, An artist's impression of Kinahan during his hearing on SundayKinahan did not have legal representation, and told the court that he did not have time to arrange this.When Judge McGrath suggested that he should be charged today and legal representation arranged later on, Kinahan replied: "If I have time, yes."Det Sgt Colm Davison told the court he arrested Kinahan earlier that evening.Judge McGrath asked Kinahan if he would like to appear at the next court sitting in person or via videolink.Kinahan asked if he had to "decide now" and it was explained to him he could make a decision later and notify the governor in the prison.Judge McGrath explained to Kinahan he could file an application for bail through the High Court.Kinahan replied: "I think we all know I won't be getting bail, but thank you for your time."'Landmark of judicial cooperation'The UAE and Ireland have an extradition treaty and on Sunday justice ministers from both jurisdictions issued a joint statement welcoming Kinahan's extradition."The Irish national is regarded as one of the most high-profile individuals sought for prosecution in connection with transnational organised crime and is accused of directing an organised crime organisation," it stated.Irish Justice Minister Jim O'Callaghan described the extradition as a "landmark of judicial cooperation between the two countries".He also commended "the professionalism, efficiency, and diligence demonstrated by the UAE judicial authorities throughout the extradition proceedings".His UAE counterpart, Abdullah bin Sultan bin Awad Al Nuaimi, said it underscored "the steadfast commitment we have to supporting global efforts to combat transnational organised crime". The extradition agreement was previously used to extradite Sean McGovern, a "senior lieutenant" in the Kinahan organised crime group.He was sentenced to 24 years in prison in June for directing the activities of a criminal organisation.What is the Kinahan cartel?According to former Garda Commissioner Drew Harris, the gang is estimated to have made more than €1bn (£857,870,000) globally from its activities.The US Treasury Department has in the past compared the gang to crime organisations such as Italy's Camorra, Mexico's Los Zetas and Japan's Yakuza.A reward of up to $5m (£3.7m) has also been offered by the US for information on Daniel, his father Christopher Snr and brother Christopher Jnr.Image source, CAROLINE QUINN/GETTY IMAGESImage caption, Gangland rivals tried to shoot Daniel Kinahan during a boxing weigh-in event in Dublin's Regency Hotel 10 years agoIn 2022, Thomas Kavanagh, who the NCA said ran the group's criminal operations in the UK, was jailed for 21 years alongside Gary Vickery and Daniel Canning, who were sentenced to 20 years and 19 and a half years respectively.The NCA said evidence showed they were responsible for cocaine imports estimated to be up to £23.4m, and cannabis imports worth about £6.4m.Kinahan himself became a target for murder and escaped an attempt on his life during a fatal shooting at a Dublin hotel in 2016.He left Ireland and spent time living in Spain and more recently in Dubai, where a warrant for his arrest was issued by the Irish courts in April. Daniel Kinahan's lawyer previously told BBC Panorama that he has no criminal record or convictions and allegations about him being a crime boss are false and have no evidential basis.

schema.headline: Daniel Kinahan: Suspected crime boss appears before Special Criminal Court

title: Could your tattoo stop you from getting a job?
description: Image source, Alyssa GrocuttImage caption, Dr Alyssa Grocutt explored perceptions of tattoos in the workplace for her PhDByEleanor LawrieSocial Affair
body: Image source, Alyssa GrocuttImage caption, Dr Alyssa Grocutt explored perceptions of tattoos in the workplace for her PhDByEleanor LawrieSocial Affairs ReporterTattoos have been in the cultural mainstream for years. Even the prime minister has got one (a bee, on his bicep).And there are no signs the trend is starting to fade. More people than ever are going under the needle as a form of self-expression: 40% of British 25-49 year-olds have at least one tattoo, according to a 2024 YouGov poll.The most popular body part to be inked? The upper arm, says YouGov.But has that acceptance carried over into the workplace?'I don't think it's totally accepted'Sociologist Dr Michael Rees says a big gulf in social acceptability remains between visible and non-visible tattoos, particularly those on  hands, neck and face as opposed to the rest of the body."I don't think it's completely accepted, and I think there's probably limits to that."While Rees himself has his hands and neck inked, he didn't get either done until he got his first permanent job as an academic."Even working in the career I work in, I was concerned that it may harm my job prospects."I think people getting tattooed in those areas are potentially restricting the careers that they go into."This is borne out by 2022 YouGov research, which found that while about two-thirds of people consider visible tattoos on the face or neck unprofessional, a similar proportion would think other visible tattoos are professional.Image source, Matthew ReesImage caption, Sociologist Dr Michael Rees has his hands and neck inked, but didn't get either done until he got his first permanent job as an academicDr Alyssa Grocutt, who is herself heavily tattooed, explored perceptions of tattoos in the workplace for her PhD at the University of Calgary in Canada, and found many stereotypes around tattooed people still exist today, both positive and negative.Perhaps unsurprisingly, people with intimidating tattoos – in this study, a skull and a knife – were perceived as risky, while those with "friendly" tattoos of a rose and some leaves were perceived as more creative and artistic.Overall, job applicants with visible tattoos are still slightly less likely to be hired than those without, she says.But for entrepreneurs, or those working in creative industries, Grocutt suggests they may be viewed as an extension of someone's personal brand."Even 11 years ago, when I started getting tattooed, the hands, neck and face were called 'job stoppers', and a lot of artists wouldn't tattoo people in those areas," she says."I think it's shifting a bit or maybe tattoo artists don't want to be gatekeepers. There's more positive perceptions now, [but] you still get a lot more attention, and that's an adjustment to get used to."From counterculture to mainstreamFor centuries, tattoos were firmly linked to criminal gangs and sailors and, more recently, counter-cultural movements such as punk and motorbike clubs.But since the early 2000s, tattoos have been steadily "demystified" through a combination of celebrities and popular TV shows such as Tattoo Fixers and London Ink, says Rees."When I got my first tattoos in the late '90s... they were outside of the mainstream. But they are everywhere now."Every tattooed person he interviewed in the 2000s for his research cited David Beckham as their inspiration; the footballer made a statement when he got his first inking in 1999. Now, celebs like Harry Styles and Ed Sheeran are covered in tattoos, with more than 50 each.'A more affordable way of becoming an art collector'Tattoo artist Martha Smith thinks stigma has "changed massively", with tattoos no longer seen as associated with criminality or class discrimination.And new trends are emerging too. Smith, who is based in Broadstairs, Kent, specialises in fine line and dot work tattoos. The hashtag #finelinetattoo has racked up 10.3m searches on Instagram, while #dotworktattoo boasts 4.8m searches."Probably until the early noughties, there was a very specific person who thought they could be tattooed. But in the 13 years I've been tattooing, clients have certainly become more diverse," Smith says, adding that she quite often tattoos NHS workers, social workers or teachers.Image source, Martha SmithImage caption, Tattoo artist Martha Smith specialises in fine line and dot work tattoos and thinks stigma has "changed massively"Catherine Hibbert, 44, waited almost 20 years to get her first tattoo. She now plans to get one every year of her forties."I was a bit nervous when I went for my first one," she says. "I was scared of it being painful, or that I was making the wrong decision.But as soon as the tattoo template was on, Hibbert says she "instantly loved it"."I guess it's an adrenaline rush, but I'm on a high for days after."Her forearm tattoo comprises geometric shapes symbolising different members and aspects of her family."They've all got meaning, and I like the fact that I can design them myself," says Hibbert, who works in an art gallery.Image source, Catherine HibbertImage caption, "I guess it's an adrenaline rush, but I'm on a high for days after," says Catherine Hibbert, who plans to get a tattoo every year of her forties  Smith thinks tattooists themselves now come from a much broader artistic background."You now often go to a tattooist because of their artwork. This massively opens up the kind of person that would want a tattoo and what a tattoo can mean. It also is a more affordable way of becoming an art collector."This chimes with how Hibbert feels."Everybody loves my arm tattoo," she says. "I think it's because it's quite unusual from what lots of people expect a tattoo to look like… this is very delicate."The value of authenticity Of all the factors behind tattoos' popularity, authenticity is the one Rees thinks trumps them all – because, he says, it is something we really value culturally."A lot of my respondents thought that was something that a tattoo gave them, a commitment to a band or to a person, to [addiction] recovery, just to kind of [being] who they really were."Of course, the elephant in the room is regret. Tattoos are permanent, and critics suggest that as these generations age they may no longer like the inkings they chose decades previously.But Hibbert says that is not a concern for her."They're like a story, so it's memories and it's stories about me and my life."

schema.headline: Could your tattoo stop you from getting a job?
